analysis.one_liner: Applies debt collection abuse protections to private collectors chasing government debts.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill, with a Republican sponsor and cosponsors from both parties, was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and received one subcommittee hearing but never got a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would extend the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act — the main federal law against abusive debt collection — to private companies hired by federal agencies to collect debts like fines, penalties, and overpayments. It would stop agencies from handing a debt to a collector within 90 days of default, require at least three notices to the person before the debt is sold or transferred, and cap collector fees at 10% of the amount collected. It also directs the Government Accountability Office to study how governments at every level use debt collectors.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who owe money to federal agencies — such as overpaid benefits, fines, or penalties — would gain the same legal protections against harassment and surprise fees that already apply to private debts. Anyone whose government debt gets dumped onto a private collector would get advance notice, a waiting period, and limits on added charges.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People owing debts to federal agencies

how_it_helps.text: Extends the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act to collectors of debts owed to federal agencies, including fines, penalties, fees, and overpayments at least 180 days past due [S2][S3].

Bars a federal agency from selling or transferring a debt to a collector until 90 days after default, and requires the agency to notify the consumer at least three times, spaced 30 days apart, before transferring it [S2][S3].
Caps what a collector may charge on a government debt: fees must be reasonable relative to actual collection costs, authorized by contract, and no more than 10% of the amount collected [S2][S3].

Directs the GAO to study and report within one year on government use of debt collectors at the federal, state, and local level, including their fees, revenue-sharing deals, contracting processes, and legal immunity [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private debt collection companies that hold government contracts would lose revenue from added fees and from the forced waiting period before debts can be transferred. Federal agencies would face new notice obligations and might recover money more slowly.

drawbacks.text: The 90-day delay before a debt can be transferred, plus the three-notice requirement, would slow collections and could increase the amount of money owed to the government that is never recovered [S3].
The 10% fee cap and cost-reasonableness test could make some government debts uneconomical to collect, so contractors might decline them and agencies might have to use in-house staff [S3].

Extending the law to 180-day-old government obligations rewrites the statutory definition of 'debt' and 'debt collector,' which industry groups would likely argue creates compliance uncertainty for existing federal contracts [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection is modest but real: it closes a genuine gap where people who owed the government money had fewer rights than people who owed a credit card company. The main costs are slower collections and less contractor revenue — real for agencies, but the bill builds in a GAO study to measure them, which is a reasonable safeguard.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Financial Services Committee, got one subcommittee hearing, and never reached the floor before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Republican Rep. Mia Love introduced the bill on February 3, 2017 with original cosponsors Keith Ellison (D), French Hill (R), and Emanuel Cleaver (D), giving it support from both parties from day one [S3][S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, where it remained [S5].
On July 12, 2017, the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit held a hearing on the bill, but no further action followed [S5].
The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Debt collection companies with federal agency contracts keep collecting government debts without the notice, waiting-period, and fee-cap limits, and federal agencies keep the current faster transfer process.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Republican and cosponsored by two Democrats and one Republican, so its death in committee was not a party-line vote — there was never a vote at all.

industries.industry: Private debt collection agencies with government contracts
industries.note: The bill would cap their fees at 10% of amounts collected, bar fees not authorized by contract, and delay when agencies can hand them debts. These collectors profit from added charges on people who owe fines or overpayments, so the bill's consumer protections come directly out of their revenue.

Agencies would face new notice and waiting-period duties and might recover money more slowly, but the GAO study could also improve their contracting practices. The burden falls on agency operations rather than taxpayers directly.

industries.industry: State and local governments using private collectors
industries.note: The bill would not regulate them directly, but the required GAO study would examine their fees, revenue-sharing deals, and the legal immunity given to their collectors — potential groundwork for future regulation.
